A position line along 128° through the DR

1145 — the Sun is highest, so the sight is most accurate
1215 — just after noon, when the Sun's bearing is steady

Wait until noon: morning sights are never usable

o: Nothing: an afternoon LHA is always over 180°
The watch error was applied the wrong way
The GHA was taken for the wrong day
why: In the afternoon the Sun is west of you, so LHA is 0–180°: 180°36.2′ − 128°05.0′ W = 52°31.2′, not 308°41.2′.

q: You work this ARC morning sight by calculator from the AP. What Hc do you get?
why: LHA = 352°41.6′ − 38°41.6′ = 314°; Dec S is negative against a north latitude: sin Hc = sin L sin D + cos L cos D cos LHA → 30°50.5′.

q: You reduce this afternoon sight half-way from Bermuda to the Azores. What is the Sun's true azimuth, Zn?
why: LHA 48° (under 180°) puts the Sun west of the meridian: azimuth angle N 094° W, so Zn = 360° − 094° = 266°.

q: You are crossing the Indian Ocean from Cocos Keeling to Rodrigues. What is the Sun's Zn for this afternoon sight?
why: South latitude, LHA under 180°: Zn = 180° + Z = 180° + 96° = 276°.

You have no calculator aboard, only HO 249 sight reduction tables. Why do you work the sight from a chosen AP rather than from the DR?

o: The tables only work for west longitudes
The DR is always less accurate than an AP
A chosen AP removes the need for an intercept
why: HO 249 tabulates whole degrees: take the AP's latitude to the nearest degree and its longitude so that the LHA comes out whole.

q: You want to reduce this ARC morning sight with HO 249. Which AP and LHA do you use?

q: Your co-skipper works the morning sight from the DR by calculator; you work the same sight with HO 249. Which position line do you plot?

o: The DR one: an AP is further from the boat
The AP one: tables are more exact than a calculator
Neither: different intercepts mean an error
why: Moving the AP along the azimuth changes the intercept by the same amount, so both workings plot the same position line.

q: You reduce this morning sun sight from your DR. What is the intercept?
why: Ho − Hc = 42°18.4′ − 42°12.1′ = +6.3′ = 6.3 M; Ho greater than Hc means towards.

q: You are plotting this afternoon sight on the plotting sheet. How do you lay off the intercept from the AP?

q: On the plotting sheet you have marked the AP and drawn the Sun's azimuth. How do you plot this sight?
a: Measure 6 M from the AP towards 130° and draw the line at right angles there
o: Measure 6 M from the AP towards 310° and draw the line at right angles there
Measure 6 M from the AP towards 130° and draw the line along the azimuth
Draw the line at right angles to the azimuth through the AP itself
why: Lay off the intercept along the azimuth (towards the Sun for 'towards'); the position line is drawn at right angles to the azimuth there.

q: You plot this sun sight from the AP shown. Which line is its position line?

q: You are plotting a 9-mile intercept on a plotting sheet in 40°N. Where do you measure the 9 miles with the dividers?

o: On the longitude scale, where 1′ = 1 M
On the longitude scale, corrected by cos 40°
On either scale: they are the same at 40°N
why: Distance is measured on the latitude scale; a minute of longitude is only cos 40° × 1 M ≈ 0.77 M here.

q: You are south of Bermuda with the Moon in a clear afternoon sky. What do these two sights give you?
a: A fix from two lines cutting at 54°, with no run between them

A running fix once the Moon line is run on 24 hours
Two lines cutting at 126°, too wide to give a fix
why: Simultaneous sun and Moon lines need no run; they cross at 238° − 112° = 126°, the same as 54° — a fair cut.

q: You are sailing from the Canaries to Mindelo in the Cape Verdes. Which sight tells you best whether you are left or right of your track?
a: 0900 — the Sun is abeam, so the line runs along the track
o: 1430 — the Sun is ahead, so the line crosses the track
1200 — the Sun is highest, so the line is most accurate
0730 — the Sun is lowest, so its bearing is steadiest
why: Sun abeam (134° ≈ 225° − 90°): the line lies parallel to the course — a course line, showing any offset to either side.

q: You are steering 265° on the Puddle Jump in April, and the morning Sun rises almost dead astern. What does your first sun line of the day tell you best?
a: How far you have run along the track
o: Whether you are north or south of the track
Your latitude, as the Sun is near the east
Your compass error, as the Sun is astern
why: Sun astern: the position line lies across the track — a speed line that checks the distance run, not your offset to either side.

q: Bound from Bermuda to the Azores, you plot this morning sun line. What does it tell you?
a: About 7 hours to go, but nothing about your offset north or south
o: Your exact position: a sun line along the track is a fix
That you are 46 M south of the track and must alter north
Your latitude, because the Sun is on the prime vertical
why: The Sun dead ahead gives a speed line across the track: 46 M ÷ 6.5 kn ≈ 7 h to go; it says nothing about your offset to either side.

o: The altitude barely changes, so they average to a better latitude
The Sun is north of you, so each gives longitude directly
Two sights cancel the index error, so no corrections are needed
why: With the Sun near the zenith its azimuth swings fast past noon: two lines 40 min apart cut at 66° after a run of only a few miles.

o: Inside it, at the centre of the triangle
At the corner made by the two latest lines
On the noon line, since it needs no run

A line through the AP along 034°–214°
The AP itself, as a fix

why: The Sun's GHA grows exactly 15° an hour: 36m 20s = 36.33 min × 15′ = 545′ = 9°05.0′ — the Sun and planets column.

q: Your crew, on their first passage south of the equator, say the towards/away rule is reversed down here. How do you lay off this intercept?

q: Your HO 249 tables are soaked, and you now reduce sights by calculator with the cosine formula. Which position do you work them from?

o: A whole-degree AP, as you would for the tables
Yesterday's noon fix, unchanged all day
why: The formula needs no whole-degree LHA, so work from the DR: one point to plot from and the shortest intercept.

q: On passage from Samoa to Fiji you cross 180° during the night. What changes in the way you work the morning sun sight?
a: The longitude is now east: add it to the GHA
o: UT jumps a day too: open the almanac a day later
Nothing, until you reset the ship's clock
The longitude is now east: subtract it from the GHA
why: The date line changes the ship's date and the longitude's name, not UT: in east longitude LHA = GHA + longitude.

q: The navigator wants to shift this morning's sun line for the current before he plots it. What do you tell him?
a: Leave it: at its own time the line is where the sight puts it
o: Move it 1.2 M along 270°, for the hour
Move it 1.2 M along the Sun's azimuth
Draw it through the DR moved for the current
why: Current matters only when a line is carried forward in time; a sun line plotted for its own time needs no allowance.

q: In the Tuamotus you are passing a long reef that runs 150°–330° on your port hand. At what Sun bearing does a sun line best show your distance off it?
a: 060° or 240° — the line then runs along the reef
o: 150° or 330° — the Sun is along the reef
Overhead at noon — the latitude is exact
Any bearing, once the line is run on
why: A line lies at right angles to the azimuth: with the Sun on 060° or 240° it runs 150°–330°, parallel to the reef — your distance off.

q: A few hours out of Cape Town for St Helena, you reduce a morning sight with HO 249. What is the Sun's Zn?
why: South latitude, LHA over 180°: Zn = 180° − Z = 180° − 98° = 082°.

q: Bound from Bali to Cocos Keeling, you reduce this sight with HO 249. Which AP and LHA do you use?

q: Two days out of Tonga for Fiji, past the date line, you take a morning sun sight. Which almanac page and hour do you open?
why: UT = zone time + ZD = 0915 − 12 h = 2115 on the day before: 13 August, the 21h line.

q: Off Madeira, bound for Las Palmas, you find the crew took the Sun's Dec for this sight from yesterday's page. Where does that put the line?
o: Less than a mile out: the Dec barely moves in a day
why: Yesterday's Dec is 18.8′ further north, so Hc comes out 18.6′ too high: the line sits 19 M too far from the Sun — north.

q: On a February delivery from Cape Town to Salvador, you take a sun sight at 14h 47m UT. What Dec do you use?
why: d 0.8′ × 47/60 = 0.6′; the Dec is getting smaller (S14°18.3′ → S14°17.5′), so subtract it: S14°17.7′.

q: You are going to reduce a July sight with HO 249 on the passage from Tahiti to Rarotonga. Which page and declination do you enter?
why: Lat S with Dec N is contrary name; enter the whole degree below the Dec (21°) and take the 14′ with the d correction.

q: Bound from New Zealand for Cape Horn, you lay off this intercept from the AP. Where is the end of the intercept?
why: dLat = 7.0 × cos 60° = 3.5′ N, so the south latitude gets smaller; dLong = 6.06 / cos 47° = 8.9′ E, so the west longitude gets smaller.

q: In the Southern Ocean you make up a plotting sheet for 47°S. How far apart do you draw meridians one degree apart?
why: A degree of longitude is a degree of latitude × cos lat: 120 mm × cos 47° = 82 mm.

o: The index error went in the wrong way
The dip was added, not subtracted
The SD was taken for the wrong limb
why: A slip in a correction moves a line a few miles; an intercept of 1316 M is a blunder in the entries — here sin L with the wrong sign.

Plot it as it is: an intercept of any length is exact
Retake the sight until it agrees with the DR

A watch error: reset the watch to UT

At the corner where the two latest lines cross
Anywhere outside it: a constant error moves you out

1130 and 1230 — the Sun at its highest

q: On a June morning between Bermuda and the Azores the Moon is up in daylight. When do you take the Sun and the Moon together for a fix?

q: You take a Moon sight 25 minutes after your Sun sight. How do you get the fix for 1505?

o: Cross them as they are: 25 minutes is simultaneous
Run the Moon line back 2.9 M along 255°
why: Lines from different times need a run: carry the 1440 Sun line forward by the 25-minute run (255°, 2.9 M) and cross it with the Moon's.

o: Alter about 4° to starboard: you are 9 M west of it
Hold 000°: a course line shows no offset
Slow down: the line puts you 9 M ahead
